body: As the accessibility of computers improves, more trained artists begin directly intervening with the machines and code, such as Joan Truckenbrod and Colette Bangert.

By the late 1960s, a highly established British painter in the London art scene, who had only recently represented Great Britain in the 1966 Venice Biennale, became interested in computers. He left London in 1968 to teach art in California, where he gained access to a CDC 3200 mainframe computer, becoming fascinated with artificial intelligence. By 1971 Harold Cohen had built a computer-controlled drawing machine, which he showed at the Fall Joint Computer Conference. In 1972, early drawings from this system were shown at LACMA in Three Behaviors for the Partitioning of Space and by 1973 he had dubbed the system AARON. This special decade thus saw the rise of AI in art from a trained painter.

The ’70s also saw Chicago become the center of the generative art universe with Sonia Landy Sheridan at School of the Art Institute of Chicago founding Generative Systems. This experimental art and technology lab had access to the latest emerging devices, enabling them to explore their creative potential.
Also in Chicago, Tom DeFanti at the University of Illinois Chicago developed GRASS at the legendary Electronic Visualization Lab that Larry Cuba used on Star Wars.
For more context, we suggest watching or listening (transcript) to our Ch 5 Artist Discussion with Joan Truckenbrod and Hans Dehlinger, featuring special guest host Anika Meier.

body: This landmark Conceptual art exhibition reinforced the dematerialization of the art object. Kynaston McShine curated Information in consultation with art historian and critic Lucy Lippard. The show examined how culture had been altered by “communications systems such as television and film and by increased mobility.” Conceptual art defined the show. Artists employed language and rules to encourage participation. The works consisted of photographs, videos and ideas, representing “the sense of mobility and change that pervades their time.“ This anticipated the coming rise of digital mass media art. The show was “interested in ways of rapidly exchanging ideas, rather than embalming the idea in an 'object'" for visual pleasure, according to McShine. It was a crucial moment in the six year period (1966-1972) identified by Lucy Lippard as the dematerialization of the art object in her watershed book, Six Years: the Dematerialization of the Art Object from 1966 to 1972. 150 artists from 15 countries participated, including Sol LeWitt, On Kawara, Joseph Beuys and Yoko Ono. The role of Information in the dematerialization of the art object was critical to the development of digital art. For McShine, the artwork wasn’t necessarily a physical object. It was "simply a method of distributing the visual information that interests the artist.”

body: Software - Information Technology: Its New Meaning for Art showcased programmed art’s potential as a creative tool. The experimental exhibition was curated by Jack Burnham. According to the catalogue, it aimed to “encourage [conceptual] artists to use the medium of electronic technology in challenging and unconventional ways.” The exhibition saw “software“ as a process that a machine or person could execute based on instructions from the artist. According to Burnham, the show provided “the means by which the public could personally respond to programmatic situations structured by artists.” The show was deeply inspired by cybernetics' interest in communication and the environment. Software presented art objects as communication devices in dialogue with a responsive audience. Participating artists included those at the forefront of technological and conceptual art: Sonia Sheridan, Allan Kaprow, Nam June Paik, Hans Haacke, and others. Nicholas Negroponte’s Architecture Machine Group, which would go on to become the MIT Media Lab (with Negroponte as director), exhibited the installation, SEEK, a life-sensing computerized system that pioneered the use of machine learning. Following the strong momentum of the '60s, Software marked a high point in the use of technology in Conceptual art. That same summer, MoMA’s Information had already gathered dozens of conceptual artists, this time with no code involved and little mention of technology. Mainstream Conceptual art had shied away from the computer and code by 1970. Yet in 1970 at Software, Conceptual art and the computer were perhaps at their zenith. It also anticipated today’s digital, instruction-based art by several decades.

body: In a sign that computer art was gaining greater acceptance and recognition, some of the movement’s leading artists participated in the first computer art exhibition at the Venice Biennale. Participating computer artists included Herbert Franke, Frieder Nake, Georg Nees, Auro Lecci and the Japanese Computer Technique Group (CTG). The pioneers’ work was included alongside modern art masters Josef Albers and Max Bill. A parallel event also included Computer music and the work of John Cage, Earle Brown and Alan Sutcliffe.

body: The Osaka Expo marked a pivotal turning point in post-war Japanese art history by marking an end to avant-garde movements and ushering in the era of new media art. Fujiko Nakaya created one of her iconic fog sculptures as part of the Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.) pavilion. She would go on to establish the Tokyo branch of E.A.T. in 1971. Billy Klüver was central to the design of The E.A.T. Pepsi-Cola Pavilion. He specifically sought to provide a participative environment that encouraged visitors to explore. The event marked what Grant Taylor describes as the beginning of the end of E.A.T.: “E.A.T. had suffered terribly at the hands of the Pepsi-Cola Company, which withdrew its support after Klüver and his colleagues had designed an intelligent environment for the company’s pavilion at the 1970 Osaka World’s Fair. This, according to [Douglas] Davis, cost EAT heavily in morale and public support. For the critics and artists, who opposed collaboration with profit-oriented firms from the start, the crisis proved their point.”

body: Sheridan founded the Generative Systems program at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago that would continue for a decade. Often combining a variety of equipment in unusual ways, she was interested in exploring the creative possibilities of the latest technology. Like today’s generative art, Sheridan’s work was process and conceptual-focused. Sheridan wrote: "Generative Systems is not primarily equipment and machines, but an idea, an approach and a process that provides new dimensions to our continuing attempts to probe and express the emotional and intellectual lives of human beings.” The Generative Systems program had access to the newest industrial communication tools like Telecopiers, thermo-faxes, computers and more. Experimenters at heart, Sheridan and her students probed the possibilities of these technological systems in unusual ways to test their artistic limits. Sheridan and the hugely influential program demonstrated the creative possibilities of digital tools combined with generative processes.

body: Originally played by hand with counters and published by Martin Gardner, Conway’s Life is the best-known two-dimensional cellular automaton. It served as a foundational concept and source of inspiration for many generative artists. Life is played on an infinite two-dimensional grid with a certain amount of occupied cells. Each generation determines whether each cell is alive or dead depending on the state of the cells that surround it. Each cell changes status each generation. Conway’s Life would have a profound affect on the field of computation and computer generated art, specifically through its influence on the use of cellular automata in complexity science. This enabled simulation modeling of an diverse range of phenomenon including insects, traffic, weather and astronomic bodies. Overall, Life has had a profound impact on generative art by inspiring artists to explore emergent behavior, pattern generation, and algorithmic systems.

body: These two books had a significant impact on views towards technology in the 1970s, challenging prevailing notions that technological progress was inherently positive and beneficial. The books encouraged a reevaluation of the relationship between humans and technology. The books marked a shift in the optimism that the art world felt in the ’60s about the future potential of art and technology. Indicative of the ’60s optimism were shows such as Cybernetic Serendipity and The Machine. With public sentiment turning against technology, the art world turned with it, and Conceptualism moved further away from the machine, as the show Information demonstrated.

body: With his article, “There Should Be No Computer Art,” Nake announced the end of his work with the medium of computers. The essay mirrored the growing pessimism surrounding technology and thus technology and art prevailing in the early ’70s. Ultimately, the essay advocates for the recognition and celebration of human artistic agency and the unique qualities that only human artists can bring to the creative process.

body: The tide was turning against computers and technology in art by 1971. Howard Wise had permanently closed. The same year one pioneer denounces the field and ends his practice in Frieder Nake, another doubles down, however, in Franke. A seminal text, Franke’s Computergraphik - Computerkunst (Computer Graphics—Computer Art) was the first comprehensive, first-hand account of computer art’s origins. The text covers the basics in the hardware, software, practice and history of the first decade of the movement. By highlighting the intersection of technology and art, the book played a pivotal role in shaping the discourse around generative art and establishing its significance as a distinct and innovative form of artistic practice. The book also helped maintain and spark additional interest in computers in art when they were rapidly becoming less fashionable. The veneer of optimism from the late ’60s and early ’70s had peaked. During, one of computer art’s first, dark periods, Franke was the light that held it together with this text.

The Sandin IP would change thinking about video art as well as computational art as it was one of the earliest modular video synthesizers. The Sandin IP would be used to be make famous works of early video art including Phil Morton’s Colorful Colorado and Spiral 5 PTL by Sandin, Tom DeFanti and Mimi Shevitz, which is in the collection of MoMA. In particular, Sandin would combine his IP with DeFanti’s GRASS to create a series of digital art masterpieces.

body: Five years in the making and organized by Maurice Tuchman, Art and Technology was an attempt to involve industrial firms (and their machinery) in the production of art. Tuchman aimed “to ‘bring together the incredible resources and advanced technology of industry with the equally incredible imagination and talent of the best artists at work today.’” Tuchman aimed to pair artists with leading technological corporations such as IBM in a residence program for a twelve week period. This gave artists the opportunity to access facilities, research, technology and equipment that would otherwise be unavailable. The resulting artwork was exhibited at LACMA in 1971. Altogether, 76 artists participated including modern masters such as Andy Warhol, Ellsworth Kelly, Dan Flavin, Donald Judd, Victor Vasarely and Roy Lichtenstein. It also included computer and generative art pioneers such as Robert Mallary, Robert Rauschenberg, Eduardo Paolozzi, Hans Haacke and Otto Piene. Any ambitious attempt to pair art and corporations was going to experience blowback and Art and Technology certainly did. Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art explains: “Max Kozloff in his Art Forum piece ‘Multimillion Dollar Art Boondoggle’ gave what [Jack] Burnham described as the ‘most vicious, inflammatory, and irrational attack ever written on the art and technology phenomenon.’ Kozloff depicted the artists involved in the ‘lavishly funded’ [Art and Technology] project held at the Los Angeles County Museum as ‘fledgling technocrats, acting out mad science fiction fantasies,’ while the ‘more sophisticated artists he envisaged as cynical opportunists.’” Despite changing political winds about the combination of technology and art, reluctance from the art world to embrace the corporatization of art and the enormous undertaking the program entailed, Art and Technology stands as a groundbreaking and visionary event that challenged traditional notions of practice, creativity and authorship.

body: Graffiti art has ancient roots but the modern form began in the '60s in the Northeastern United States. By the early '70s in New York, young people were writing their names and street numbers across the city. Particularly famous is the TAKI 183 tag. While not the first to appear (TAKI began around 1969), it was one of the first to gain widespread attention due to a 1971 New York Times article. Graffiti art plays an important role in the story of digital generative art. First, they share much of the same genealogy. Both have roots in the origins of digital art such as the increased focus on audience participation in the '50s and '60s. Kinetic artists in the '50s such as Yaacov Agam, Pol Bury and Jesús Rafael Soto began creating 3D, geometric and interactive sculptures. The ’60s saw New Tendencies, happenings and conceptualism push to bring art out of the realm of museums. They sought to bring art on to the streets and further involve the audience. Graffiti is a direct result of this growing impulse. Graffiti also continued these traditions. As a form of urban-scale environmental art, it espouses art’s social accessibility and increased interactivity. It was thus a step toward the digital art we know today. Finally, graffiti art has strong ties to web3 art culture. The similarities include: -a strong community ethos -pseudonymous artists -digital avatars -the artist as community leader -challenging the social order

body: With Cubic Limit I (1972-1975), Mohr begins his hallowed work focusing on the cube. He created an alphabet of signs from the twelve lines of a cube. He then used programs to combine, rotate and generate these signs to create images. Noteworthy works include P-155 Cubic Limit (1974-76), which was exhibited at the 1986 SIGGRAPH exhibition, A Retrospective. Despite the similarity in content, style and subject to Sol LeWitt’s exploration of the cube in the mid-70s, Mohr’s work never received close to the critical attention “on the grounds of its computational basis,” according to Grant Taylor.

body: A key text in the development of chaos theory and thus twentieth-century science, Lorenz “was the first to recognize what is now called chaotic behavior in the mathematical modeling of weather systems.” Chaos theory would play a critical role in the development of generative art according to academic Phil Galanter. Galanter stresses the role of systems in generative art and proposes a way to classify generative systems in terms of order and disorder based on chaos theory. Chaos theory and generative art are intertwined through the exploration of complex systems and the creation of dynamic, unpredictable patterns. Chaos theory studies the behavior of nonlinear systems, emphasizing sensitivity to initial conditions and the emergence of unpredictable outcomes. Generative art leverages algorithms and rule-based processes to generate artwork that evolves organically, often exhibiting complexity and self-similarity. By embracing chaos and randomness as creative forces, generative art can harness the principles of chaos theory to produce visually captivating and unique pieces.

Kubota’s experimental approach combined performance, technology, and personal narratives, creating visually striking and thought-provoking works. She explored themes of identity, feminism, and the relationship between nature and technology. Her influential video sculptures, installations, and performances paved the way for future generations of video artists, inspiring them to merge the personal with technology.

body: A pioneer of electronic gaming, Nolan Bushnell commissioned Pong from the engineer Al Alcorn. Pong, one of the first successful video games of all time, introduced the world to interactive electronic entertainment. Beyond its technological impact, Pong also had artistic significance, blurring the lines between art and technology and showcasing the creative potential of digital media as a medium for artistic expression. Pong’s success demonstrated that video games could be more than just entertainment; they could be a form of interactive art, inspiring future generations of artists to explore the aesthetics, storytelling and interactivity within the realm of video games and media art.

body: GRASS (Graphics Symbiosis System) is simply put one of the most important advancements in computer graphics, well, ever, but especially of the 1970s. Combined with Dan Sandin's Image Processor and others, it transformed the capabilities of computers. It gave them the ability to animate in real time on a screen, something dreamed of since the days of oscillographs.

Completed as DeFanti’s doctoral work at Ohio State University, this landmark early computer animation language that was used by Larry Cuba to produce the graphics for the training sequence for the Rebel attack on the Death Star in Star Wars. Cuba would work on GRASS with DeFanti at the University of Illinois Chicago beginning in 1975. Copper Giloth worked on GRASS doing simulations of water sculptures for a friend experimentally.

DeFanti wrote GRASS in Charles Csuri’s Computer Graphics Research Group, supported by Csuri’s 1971 National Science Foundation grant for real-time film animation. It ran on the group’s PDP-11/45 with a Vector General display.

body: AARON, the autonomous drawing machine Cohen named at Stanford in 1973, pioneered the use of AI to create art. With his seminal 1973 essay “Parallel to Perception: Some Notes on the Problem of Machine-Generated Art,” Harold Cohen articulated his efforts to develop “autonomous art-making behavior” that was inventive and could “conjure meaning.” Cohen differentiated this “autonomous art-making” from computer art, which he did not highly regard, claiming that “'computer art' can barely claim consideration as art at all.” Cohen’s collaboration with AARON as a human-machine collaboration lasted 40 years and demonstrated a machine’s ability to make creative choices. His ideas and concepts for these coming decades can be found in this paper. Image is copyrighted by The Artist and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

body: The seminal work of Brazilian video and computer art pioneer, Analivia Cordeiro, M 3x3 is not only a work of generative choreography, it is also a work of video art. The piece syncs the movements of the cameras with the dancers who wear abstract geometric outfits in black and white. M 3x3 anticipates the merging of technology and dance while criticizing Brazil’s military dictatorship at the time. It also serves as a continual commentary on the influence of technology and society. body: INTERACT: MACHINE: MAN: SOCIETY was an “eventibition” that took place over five days at Edinburgh University. It included papers, a conference and an exhibition of creative computer graphics, generative dance/choreography, cybernetics and poetry. The “eventibition” featured artists such as Manfred Mohr, CAYC, Alan Sutcliffe, Manuel Barbadillo and Greta Monach. The Computer Arts Society (CAS), founded in 1968 by Alan Sutcliffe, George Mallen and John Lansdown, has aimed to explore the role of digital and electronic media in the arts for decades. After a hiatus from 1985 to 2004, CAS experienced a renaissance, preserving computer-generated art history and becoming part of the Victoria and Albert Museum’s collections. In 2024, CAS actively promotes digital media through events, exhibitions, and the annual Electronic Visualisation & the Arts (EVA) conference.

body: On the cutting edge, the Alto had a bitmapped screen and pioneered the graphics-based display, mouse, windows and icons that later systems inherited. It was never sold commercially and only 2,000 units were made, yet it was hugely influential particularly with upcoming personal computing breakthroughs like Apple’s Macintosh and Microsoft’s Windows. The Alto also signaled the growing accessibility of computers. Freed from the confines of government agencies and large corporations, computers were becoming accessible to artists directly. This enabled traditionally trained artists to begin explorations with computers, including Lillian Schwartz. Thus, the Alto would significantly impact the future of computer generated art and digital art as we know it by shaping its core design and facilitating its greater accessibility.

body: Inspired by hardware store paint color charts, this painting’s composition was determined by a randomly generated algorithm. This piece is part of a series started by Richter in the 1960s. They are related to the color collage work of Ellsworth Kelly, which Richter was unaware of at the time. Richter and Kelly’s algorithmic explorations of color and form stand as critical examples of material generative art’s importance and rich history.

body: Hugely important and later renamed the Experimental and Computing Department and lasting until 1981, the department introduced computer and video fine art to the Slade School of Fine Art at University College London, influenced by Slade staff member titans and students such as Harold Cohen, Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi. The Department marked a critical leap into the field of technology in by the art school. It was a rarity among traditional art schools, particularly in the UK. Independent Group figures including Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi had trained at the Slade, and Harold Cohen taught painting there from 1961 to 1968. William Coldstream, Slade Professor from 1950 to 1975, provided significant assistance for the Experimental and Computing Department, building on his experience at the General Post Office Film Unit in the 1930s. Harold Cohen, who was quite as a successful painter before turning to computer art, contributed to this technological revolution with early works that demonstrated an interest in systems and logical processes. Malcolm Hughes, co-founder of the Systems group in 1969, played a crucial role in launching the new Slade department, which reflected Constructivism. Additional students from the department include artists such as Paul Brown, Stephen Bell, Stephen Scrivener and Dominic Boreham would study under Hughes at the Slade.

body: Lucy Lippard’s book Six Years: The Dematerialization of the Art Object from 1966 to 1972 was a seminal publication that had a significant influence on contemporary generative art. Lippard’s book chronicled the emerging conceptual art movement, emphasizing the importance of ideas and processes over traditional art objects. Her focus on the dematerialization of art and the emphasis on concepts, systems and participation laid the foundation for generative art’s exploration of algorithmic and rule-based processes. In particular, the notion of a dematerialized art object has been critical to the contemporary understanding of art and its connection to the blockchain and NFTs. These instruments enable digital ownership. Lippard’s book also encouraged artists to embrace new technologies and computational methods, leading to the development of generative art practices that prioritize dynamic, interactive, and generative systems. Six Years served as a catalyst for redefining artistic practice and expanding the possibilities of art beyond materiality, inspiring generations of generative artists to experiment with digital technologies and dynamic processes.

body: Founded by Thomas DeFanti and Dan Sandin, the Electronic Visualization Lab (EVL) is still in existence today. EVL is a research lab at the University of Illinois at Chicago focused on computer science and advanced technologies. It specializes in collaborative visualization, virtual reality and data science. Over the years, they’ve created innovative technologies like the CAVE virtual reality system (90s) and SAGE graphics environment (2000s). They work on connecting scientists and engineers with tools to visualize complex data, allowing them to gain insights. EVL also collaborates globally and is supported by organizations like the National Science Foundation, National Institutes of Health and more.

body: Occurring during the National Sciences Foundation Workshop on Computer Graphics in Boulder, Colorado, the inaugural SIGGRAPH (Special Interest Group on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques) conference, held in July 1974, marked a pivotal moment in the intersection of art and technology. Bob Schiffman and Jon Meads organized the event because they decided it had been too long since a dedicated computer graphics conference had been held. They then decided to piggy back on the larger NSF conference. The conference and its subsequent iterations would bring together researchers, artists, and industry professionals to showcase and discuss advancements in computer graphics and interactive techniques. SIGGRAPH provided a platform for the exchange of ideas, the presentation of groundbreaking computer-generated artworks and the establishment of a community focused on merging art and technology. The inaugural SIGGRAPH conference set the stage for future conferences and played a crucial role in shaping the history of art and technology, fostering collaboration, innovation, and the growth of computer-generated art.

body: TV Buddha remains one of Paik’s signature works, a video sculpture consisting of a seated Buddha facing a television screen where it watches an image of itself. The work touches on themes of surveillance, East and West, past and present, religion and technology and the viewer’s role in an artwork. TV Buddha confronts the viewer with the juxtaposition of an ancient statue and its real-time image on a television screen, exploring the relationship between tradition and technology. TV Garden, another seminal video installation by Paik which was staged at the Guggenheim in 2000, consists of densely placed live plants with TV screens hidden throughout. The work merges technology and nature by surrounding viewers with a forest of televisions, contrasting the digital and physical realms. These immersive environments aimed to challenge traditional notions of art and introduced the concept of interactive and multi-sensory experiences. The groundbreaking installations not only showcased the creative potential of technology in art but also laid the foundation for the exploration of generative systems, interactivity and the fusion of digital and analog mediums that characterize digital generative art today.

body: According to Jasia Reichardt and Grant Taylor, the 1970s marked the era of the artist-programmer. The practitioners of computer art began shifting away from the engineers and scientists who began the movement a decade earlier. From the early ’70s it was being pushed forward according to Frank Dietrich in Taylor when “a growing breed of technological artists with hybrid capabilities started to appear.” Traditionally trained artists had access to computers for the first time as their access improved. The field was no longer dominated by those in control of very expensive and often secretive large machines. Further, Taylor writes how “Reichardt announced in 1974, ‘The bridges between art and science are finally only built by those who embody something of the two disciplines.’” The concept would permeate the computer art of the ’70s where artists saw themselves as modern-day Renaissance artists, combining scientific advancements and art, in the spirit of Leonardo da Vinci, the artist-engineer.

body: A landmark work of feminist art made from 1974 to 1979, this installation consists of a large, triangular shaped banquet table set with symbolic place settings representing 39 historically significant women. The work challenges the preciousness and permanence of fine art while its mixed media and collaborative, conceptual nature mirror trends in digital art.

body: This audiovisual work of “video noise” was created by the electronic art pioneers Steina and Woody Vasulka who co-founded The Kitchen in 1971 where they helped non-technical artists incorporate technology into their practice. Noisefileds is the result of experimentation with modulators and video synthesizers in an attempt to build a visual vocabulary for their electronic images. This pioneering work explored the creative potential of analog video synthesis, manipulating electronic signals to generate abstract and dynamic visual compositions. Noisefields showcased the possibilities of real-time signal manipulation and the emergence of electronic aesthetics. The Vasulkas' experimentation with video and electronic systems laid the foundation for subsequent artists to explore generative processes, interactivity and the fusion of technology and art.

body: Deemed “decades ahead of its time” by Casey Reas, Krueger developed Videoplace for nearly twenty years. This interactive computer system allowed users to engage with virtual environments through body movements and gestures. Built first with video alone, and with computer vision added over the following decade, Videoplace pioneered the concept of real-time interactive video art, blurring the line between the physical and digital worlds. Its influence on digital generative art lies in its exploration of user participation, interactivity and the creation of dynamic, responsive visual experiences.

body: Molnár developed “Molnart” with her husband François Molnár between the years 1974 and 1976. The software program enabled engagement in expérimentation picturale systématique (“systematic pictorial experimentation”). The program, written in FORTRAN, required a high capacity computer connected to a display screen and plotter. Molnart aimed to disrupt the monotony of regular, geometric patterns, achieving various “satisfactory…aesthetic states” by systematically modifying inputs step by step. Vera Molnár applies various techniques such as removing squares randomly, changing the probability of appearance for different-sized squares, introducing color and incorporating human-like irregularities. This approach was essentially what Molnár used to achieve (Dés)Ordres (1974). The generated images could then be drawn on paper. Vera Molnár reflects on the aesthetic qualities of the computer-generated images compared to hand-drawn ones and explores the possibilities of combining different methods.

body: This comprehensive exploration of the intersection between science, technology and the arts provides a captivating journey into various disciplines, including visual arts, music, theater, film and literature, to reveal the profound influence of scientific advancements on artistic expression. Kranz’s work reads as a reflection of a decade (the ’60s) that both he and the artists he covers are responding to the vast social, technological and political developments. It covers topics such as digital art, artificial life, interactive installations and multimedia performances, showcasing the transformative power of science and technology in shaping contemporary artistic practices.

Derived from a course taught by Cooper at MIT, “Messages and Means,” the Visible Language Workshop (VLW) took a multi-disciplinary approach to design. It specifically examined interactive design, photography, typesetting and platemaking. The VLW would prove to be highly influential to both Casey Reas and Zach Lieberman in their creations of Processing and openFrameworks respectively. “The VLW was well-connected to both the Center for Advanced Visual Studies and the Architecture Machine Group; and it was one of the original research groups of the Media Lab at its founding in 1985.”

body: Eno’s album Discreet Music employed techniques for randomness to compose generative music that resemble and build upon the work of artists such as John Cage, Terry Riley and Steve Reich. The album introduced the approach Eno would later call “generative music,” where musical compositions are created through rule-based processes rather than traditional composition methods. Eno utilized tape loops, delays, and ambient textures to create an evolving and infinitely variable sonic landscape. This approach challenged the notion of fixed, linear music, emphasizing the exploration of emergent and unpredictable outcomes in both music and visual art.

body: Organized by Grace C. Hertlein, ICCH/2 was the largest computer art exhibition held in the United States at that point. It showcased computer made film, graphics and music. The show also marked a turning point in the use of the computer for art. According to Hertlein, “In earlier exhibitions, physicists, systems analysts and programmers dominated this field. Today’s computer artists are sculptors, painters and architects who use the computer primary as a designing aid.” The aesthetics of computer art were changing as well. Hertlein viewed earlier computer art exhibitions, including the most famous of them all, Cybernetic Serendipity, as “overly preoccupied with mathematics and line.”

body: Benoit Mandelbrot coined the term fractal while working at IBM. Using computer generated images to illustrate his mathematically derived concepts, he was consolidating hundred of years of mathematical theory. Fractals, infinitely complex geometric patterns that exhibit self-similarity at various scales, include the Mandelbrot set, created with the iterative process where a specific pattern is repeated again and again. Mandelbrot’s groundbreaking work provided artists with a visual language to explore and create intricate, organic and visually captivating compositions. Fractals became a cornerstone of generative art, inspiring artists to use algorithms and iterative processes to generate complex and evolving imagery. The introduction of fractals revolutionized the aesthetic possibilities in digital art, fostering a deeper appreciation for the beauty of mathematical structures and the integration of science and art in the digital realm.

body: One of this story’s greatest legends. Kawaguchi will go on to win the 2010 ACM SIGGRAPH Distinguished Artist Award for Lifetime Achievement. But his creative career began around this time in the late ’70s.
In 1975 Kawaguchi, one of Japan’s most revered generative artists and animators, began developing his famous GROWTH Model, a procedural algorithm that mimics organic growth and reproduction.
Continuing to work with organic forms throughout his career, Kawaguchi showed his organic growth animations at SIGGRAPH from 1982.

Kawaguchi’s GROWTH model—described as “a self-organizing approach to developing a formative algorithm of a complex life form”—in many ways pioneered artificial life and evolutionary art. His work comes nearly a decade before fellow Artificial Life pioneers William Latham and Karl Sims.
Kawaguchi goes widely unrecognized as an artificial life pioneer despite this early work from the ’70s in the budding field.

The responses she then compiled into a book. “Some of the authors address the questions in their articles; some do not. Many of the papers are purely statements about the artist’s work. Just as the artists' artwork differs, so do their papers.” The book stands as a treasure trove of information on artistic practice with computers by some of the time’s most distinguished artists. Leavitt includes artists such as Vera Molnár, Lillian Schwartz, John Whitney and Hiroshi Kawano.

body: Held at the gallery of the Polytechnic of Central London, Molnár’s Transformations is a series of 21 drawings plotted in black ink on white paper on a Benson plotter. Each image depicts a 5x5 grid of closely drawn concentric squares. The first image in the series is perfectly uniform, with crisply drawn concentric squares orderly presented in a perfect grid. Disorder is introduced to each subsequent iteration. Finally, image 21 resembles a scribbled mess with a barely recognizable grid. The entire series is now held in the Tate collection.

body: Hertlein’s Computer Graphics and Art played a crucial role in the development of generative art history. The journal provided a platform for artists, researchers and technologists to showcase and exchange ideas about computer-generated art. It documented the evolving landscape of generative art, featuring articles, interviews and examples of innovative artworks. The journal served as a catalyst for the growth of generative art by fostering a community and facilitating the dissemination of knowledge and techniques. It thereby helped establish generative art as a recognized field, influencing subsequent generations of artists and contributing to the expansion and exploration of generative practices in the art world.

body: Apple Computer Company was founded on 1 April 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne, with the goals of making computers more user-friendly for a mass market. The company’s first product was the Apple I, which they built in Jobs’s garage, selling the device for $666.66 without a monitor or keyboard. They produced 200 units which did not even sell out after 9-10 months. The Apple I was the predecessor to the iconic Apple II which would be released the following year. This moment marks an important step in the computers’ increasing accessibility, including with artists, that would only be amplified with Apple’s more successful release of the Apple II in the following year.

body: This seemingly benign event marks the beginning of what I argue is one of the most significant shifts in the history of human thinking: our love affair with digital devices. These devices, made for the home, ushered in an era marked by a new relationship with digital devices and computers. VHS (Video Home System) allowed for the playing and recording of analog video on cassettes invented by the Japanese company. The technology set off the maturation of mass media, enabling digital media to enter people’s homes on a mass scale for the first time. As these devices entered homes, society’s perception of computers significantly altered, as an inscrutable, blackbox, previously associated with war became as close to use as family and friends. VHS machines would be followed by similarly tectonic events that continue this progression of mass media entering the home, including the 1977 release and widespread success of the Apple II, igniting the personal computer era. This was instantly followed by the introduction of the video game console the same year with the Atari 2600. In 1976 Shugart Associates introduced the 5.25-inch floppy disk drive and diskette. This would become the vital storage device for computers in general as well as computer art and digital art in the 1980s. Finally, the same year would see the introduction of the LaserDisc, the first commercially successful optical storage device, which would also store digital art such as Lynn Hershmann Leeson’s Lorna.

body: Mohr produced this series of computer-generated drawings from 1977, within the Cubic Limit II phase. The series consisted of images of deconstructed single cubes. Dissected, the cubes were not symmetrical. This concept of broken symmetry has roots in the work of Renaissance artist, Leonardo da Vinci, who was hugely influential in this decade as the embodiment of the artist-scientist. Lillian Schwartz a decade later would explore this topic more explicity in her Mona/Leo, which bisects the face of the Mona Lisa and combines it with the visage of da Vinci. body: This master’s thesis, Computergrafik, Ein Lehr- und Lernbuch (“Computer graphics, a text and learning book”), was a survey of computer graphics. It also published in detail SNE (COMP) ART, one of the first art machines based on parameters. The code was significant as SNE ART became a way to enhance generative art’s accessibility. It was used to teach the field (using FORTRAN). Nearly 40 years later in 2013, Dietrich M. Scheringer would bring SNE ART to Processing, based on the original FORTRAN code.

One of the first mass-produced “microcomputers,” the Apple II helped begin the personal computer crazy in the late 1970s, revolutionizing computing and computer art forms. It would also help kick of the Demoscene as one of the first devices to attract cracker crews. With its accessible hardware and user-friendly interface, the Apple II democratized computing and provided artists with a powerful tool for creating generative artworks. The computer’s graphics and sound capabilities, along with the availability of programming languages like BASIC, enabled artists to experiment with algorithms and create interactive visual and audio experiences. The Apple II represented an exponential jump in computer popularity and accessibility as between 1977 and 1984, over 2 million units sold. The Apple II’s popularity and widespread adoption also fostered a growing community of artists exploring generative art.

body: This paper conceived of the laptop and tablet computers decades before their existence. It outlines the goals and developments of Kay and Goldberg’s “dream” to create a portable computer the size of a “notebook,” which they called the Dynabook. Mock-ups of the Dynabook were decades ahead of their time. It looked more like a tablet than today’s “notebook” computers. The device was designed for artists in particular, as its sketch pad like design facilitated hand drawing and painting. It also theoretically included software for the creation of animation and music. It wasn’t until after a decade of early attempts in the 1980s that Apple would produce the PowerBook in 1991 and IBM the ThinkPad in 1992 that the vision of the Dynabook even started to be fulfilled. It was not until 2010 that Apple would introduce the iPad

body: This book chapter by one of the founders of computer art would have a significant impact on the development of 3D computer graphics in the coming decades. body: PostScript, which would go on to influence the Processing language created by Casey Reas and Ben Fry 25 years later, was developed by Dr John Warnock at PARC, Xerox’s research arm.
The PostScript language was built to “to communicate complex graphic printing instructions to digital laser printers.”

Warnock attempted to develop PostScript, then known as Interpress at PARC but was turned down. He then, along with Charles M. ‘Chuck’ Geschke, founded the company Adobe to rival Interpress, developing PostScript at Adobe as a robust, geometric procedural language that was more than just software to control printers.
They released PostScript finally in 1984.

body: The Third Mind is published by Beat writer William Burroughs and the artist/poet/inventor Brion Gysin. This collection of experimental cut-up writings and essays investigates the technique popularized by Burroughs, inspired in part by the interpolation of diverse sources and voices in T.S. Eliot’s The Waste Land, and explored earlier in the 1966 short film “The Cut Ups,” by Burroughs and director Antony Balch. Burroughs believed cutting up and rearranging fragments of language was a way to unlock the true meaning of a text, and said, “When you cut into the present the future leaks out.”
-Sasha Stiles

body: From Smith’s 1978 Technical Memo No. 7 at the New York Institute of Technology’s Computer Graphics Lab: “Paint is a menu-driven computer program for handpainting two-dimensional images in full color. It is a highly interactive software package with which a human artist may employ the power of a digital computer to compose paintings which are entirely of [their] own creation.” Paint would go on to serve as a prototype for subsequent graphic design software. As one of the earliest software tools for digital painting, it revolutionized the artistic process by providing artists with a digital canvas and a range of tools for creating and manipulating images. Paint allowed artists to explore new possibilities for expression, enabling them to experiment with color, texture and composition in ways that were not previously achievable. Paint’s user-friendly interface and intuitive controls democratized digital art creation, opening the doors for artists to embrace the potential of digital tools and techniques in generative art.
This pioneering work of video art saw Latham commenting on the inherently fragmented nature of video. The work features extensively manipulated and processed visuals showcasing this fragmentation.

Latham explores the blending perceptions of herself and her creations, highlighting the interconnected nature of video, storytelling and identity formation, where fact and fiction intertwine to shape one’s identity.

Latham’s creation is a video persona that is something distinct from her true self. The piece anticipates the growing tension between video art and identity, which contemporary artists like Maya Man explore.

body: An extension of Defanti’s GRASS, ZGRASS was used for generating 3D imagery and developed to be used on smaller, personal computers and gaming devices. In an effort to better control images and make electronic visualization easier, Thomas DeFanti developed ZGRASS with Jay Fenton and Nola Donato for the Bally Home Library Computer. It would go on to be used as a programming language for artists and educators in the 1980s. For example, pioneering animation artist Larry Cuba completed his film Calculated Movements on ZGRASS. Victor Acevedo would use it for his experiments in the mid ’80s he told Peter Bauman via a call 11 July 2023. Copper Giloth was the first artist to work with ZGRASS.

body: Sparking the first video game craze, the release of Space Invaders was followed by Asteroids (1979) and Pac-Man (1980). The released helped to popularize the arcade, which would have an enormous impact on not only digital aesthetics (to this day) but also how a generation of young artists would grow up viewing machines, digital art and computers. Gone were the years of the 1960s (less than 20 years prior) when computers were enigmatic with strong associations with the military, war, the powerful and questionable ethics. Very few people had ever seen one let alone knew how to interact one. In the course of eighteen years, the relationship between machine and human had changed profoundly. Children from Japan to the United States began growing up with computers in their homes. They began to interact with them and spend hours forming an intimate bond with the machine, having a profound impact on the history of any digital art.

body: “With electronics, a progressive element has entered our technical world, whose influence is not limited to industry and research, but intervenes in all areas of life. This has set in motion a development that opens up astonishing and fantastic aspects, but in other respects also arouses criticism and scepticism.” So begins Herbert W. Franke’s opening text, introducing Ars Electronica. The first edition of the now iconic event, co-founded by Hannes Leopoldseder, Hubert Bognermayr, Herbert W. Franke and Ulrich Rützel, in new media art which continues to this day, annually. Its base is now the Ars Electronica Center (AEC), a museum complex in Linz. While now a new media art institution, its beginnings in 1979 were more humble. Back then, the event was only every two years and was a part of the larger International Bruckner Festival, a Linz music festival. There was also no Prix Ars Electronica until 1987 when the now prestigious award was first handed out.

body: Jim Blinn’s simulation of the Voyager Probe’s flyby of Jupiter for NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) would have a significant impact on the development of digital art history. Blinn’s groundbreaking work utilized computer graphics techniques to visualize complex astronomical data, creating a realistic and immersive experience for scientists and the public. This pioneering use of computer graphics for scientific visualization reimagined digital art as it was known and demonstrated the potential of technology in communicating scientific concepts. David Em, JPL’s artist in residence since 1977, was introduced to Blinn’s work there, and the classically trained painter matured in his computer art style, developing works from the same year such as Transjovian Pipeline and Nora. Em would even name works after Blinn, including the piece Dr. Jim, Number 1. Blinn’s work paved the way for future collaborations between artists and scientists, shaping the field of digital art history and advancing the use of computer-generated imagery in various disciplines.

body: Larry Cuba was a computer animation pioneer of the generation that directly followed John Whitney Sr. In 1975 Whitney invited Cuba to be the programmer on Arabesque.

Earlier in the 1970s Cuba worked with Thomas DeFanti on GRASS. He also worked with George Lucas on Star Wars, providing the animation for the Death Star attack training sequence. A 4k version of the original Two Space can be viewed here. The film was completed with Defanti’s GRASS and according to the artwork description it:

“systematically explores symmetries used by Islamic artists to create abstract temple decorations. The two dimensional patterns, like the tile patterns of Islamic temples, are generated by performing a set of symmetry operations (translations, rotations, and reflections) upon a basic figure or tile.”

body: The artist describes Lorna, made from 1979 to 1984, as the first artwork to use laserdisc technology, and as an early interactive video art disc. Exploiting the interactive capabilities of the medium, the artist enables users to explore and intervene in the world of an agoraphobic woman named Lorna.”

The work highlights the continued importance of interactivity in digital art with roots to cybernetics. Lorna stands as an important example of early digital mass media art, consisting of artists releasing work on digital media that could be distributed easily around the world. According to Casey Reas, the rise of digital mass media is one of the pre-conditions for NFTs.

body: The history of AI is a story of disillusionment. The reasons to get excited (and afraid) are easy enough to predict and see coming. The problem is time frame and so often theory and ideas had to wait (decades typically) for other fields to advance while their ideas were considered dead and disproven. History praises the true believers like Geoff Hinton who stuck with it through thick and thin. What about the field's apostates?
Perhaps no figure in this story represents disillusionment and renunciation as precisely as Terry Winograd.

His story overlaps with an early goal of the AI field: a machine that genuinely understood natural language the way people do. Why should humans spend so much time learning machine languages? Shouldn't they learn ours instead?

Well, the issue is there are different ways of going about this task and two tracks had already settled by early 1970s, learning and rules. But since the incredibly damaging blow to the learning side of Minsky's Perceptrons in the previous year, the rules side (symbolic, expert systems AI) was having a moment.

Emblematic of that moment for expert systems was Winograd's SHRDLU. Between 1968 and 1970, Terry Winograd wrote SHRDLU at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. A user typed English on a teletype, while the program could "reply" in a very limited way. It was a simple robot with only a hand and an eye that could move blocks, pyramids and a box shown on a display screen. But that was about it. It was an expert system after all. Every outcome and scenario and answer had to be anticipated and baked in.

There was a lot of confusion. It asked which pyramid was meant when an order was unclear and even tried to account for its actions. Pressed on why it had stacked three blocks, it answered, “BECAUSE YOU ASKED ME TO.”
The name you ask? It spells the second column of keys on a Linotype typesetting machine.

Perhaps because of the clear and obvious limitation of expert systems, Winograd eventually abandoned the field entirely, rejecting it in a detailed and fundamental way. In a 1986 book with Fernando Flores, Understanding Computers and Cognition, Winograd and Flores argued that the task Winograd had spent decades on would be a failure even if it were to ever succeed. That's because, they argued, even fluent-seeming machines could never actually understand because they lacked embodiment and participation in life.

img.credit: Linotype keyboard showing the ETAOIN SHRDLU key rows. CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: A legendary piece that sits in MoMA, Pixillation is one of the most famous works of computer-generated film. The piece is by icons Lillian Schwartz and Ken Knowlton made at none other than Bell Labs in Murray Hill, New Jersey.
Pixillation is a short film that alternates computer-generated mosaics made with Knowlton's EXPLOR language with hand-animated sequences, set to music by Gershon Kingsley on the Moog synthesizer.

Schwartz colored the black-and-white computer output through the optical printer, giving the film a vivid, shifting palette. It was among the first films to combine computer animation and traditional techniques as art.

cite.label: Lillian Schwartz and Ken Knowlton, Pixillation, 1970. Photograph, Victoria and Albert Museum, London.

img.cap: Ken Knowlton (right), Schwartz's collaborator on Pixillation, with Golan Levin in 2007.
img.credit: Golan Levin and Ken Knowlton, Getty Museum, 2007. CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: Some people are programmed to think differently, the people whose ideas change the paradigm. The field of AI lost one of those and one of its best too soon in 1971 when Frank Rosenblatt died in a boating accident in Chesapeake Bay.

It was the afternoon of July 11, 1971, his 43rd birthday. The story goes that Rosenblatt had taken some students who were inexperienced sailors out on his sailboat. When Rosenblatt accidentally fell in the water, he was unable to be rescued.
As readers of this timeline know, the man is a bit of a hero, certainly a legend. He was the cybernetic lone wolf who was right all along, the unjustly accused.

He was the inventor of the first working neural network. In 1958, at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory, he described the Perceptron, an electronic device built on biological principles that could learn. He extended the approach in Principles of Neurodynamics.

The man certainly had ideas. He was experimental and from 1966, in Cornell’s Section of Neurobiology and Behavior. There he tested whether learned behavior could pass from trained rats to untrained ones through injections of brain extract. Umm.

He is so revered to this day, as the IEEE established an award named after him in 2004, the Frank Rosenblatt Award. It is awarded annually for "computational intelligence" and has since gone to another generation of legends, like Teuvo Kohonen, John Hopfield, Geoffrey Hinton and Paul Werbos.

img.cap: Frank Rosenblatt as a young student.
img.credit: Frank Rosenblatt as a student. CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: If you started from first principles, could you solve the world with only logic? Yeah probably not.

Remember how before we said (the split after Perceptrons) that this period in AI history was a boom time for symbolic, rules-based AI (and a subsequent winter for cybernetic, learning, connectionist AI)? Well, here is another example of "experts" trying to get expert systems to work: STRIPS.
Richard Fikes and Nils Nilsson of SRI presented STRIPS, the Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver, at the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in London in September 1971.

Built for SRI’s robot research, it described the world in first-order logic and each action as an operator with a precondition, a delete list of facts that may stop being true and an add list of facts that become true. It then searched for a sequence of operators reaching the goal. Asked to gather three boxes in one place, it returned four steps: go, push, go, push.
Unlike others from this period, STRIPS had lasting power. The Planning Domain Definition Language, a community standard since 1998, has STRIPS at its core.

img.cap: A page of Fikes and Nilsson's 1971 STRIPS paper.
img.credit: Richard E. Fikes and Nils J. Nilsson, “STRIPS: A New Approach to the Application of Theorem Proving to Problem Solving,” Artificial Intelligence 2 (1971). Page from the paper, Nils Nilsson's Stanford site.

body: After Minsky's Perceptrons, terms like "neural network" had become akin to rude words in the "West," particularly for funding. They were more accepted, however, in places like U.S.S.R. and Japan. Those areas would contribute in fundamental ways to the connectionist tradition in the '70s, often only to have their work rediscovered (and reattributed) in the '80s and '90s as the West paid closer attention.
Here is one such example of the U.S.S.R. keeping the learning torch lit in a time of otherwise darkness.

In 1971 Vladimir Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis of Moscow’s Institute of Control Sciences published in Theory of Probability and Its Applications the full proofs of a result they had announced in 1968.

It set out when the frequencies observed in one sample converge to the true probabilities across a whole class of events at once, generalizing the law of large numbers. For learning, that tells when a rule chosen for making the fewest errors on training examples will also hold on new cases. Vapnik and Chervonenkis's proofs rested on a measure of a model class's capacity, now known as the VC dimension. Their theory became a popular way to analyze neural networks moving forward.

img.cap: A diagram of how a straight line can split three points every possible way, the idea behind the VC dimension.
img.credit: Shattering example for the VC dimension of linear classifiers. Via Wikimedia Commons.

body: What this timeline (and history generally) teaches again and again is that nothing is the beginning. Everything has a predecessor and context. But some events participate in "beginning-ness" more than others we can say. And in many ways Charles Csuri's Computer Graphics Research Group (CGRG) kicked off the field of computer graphics and animation as disciplines.
Even other "beginnings" like Tom DeFanti and Dan Sandin in Chicago's EVL point back to this beginning. But of course this isn't quite the actual beginning.

In 1969 Charles Csuri received a National Science Foundation grant to study the computer’s role in research and education in the visual arts. Not such an easy award for an artist to receive smack in the middle of the Space Race, Cold War and Vietnam War. But Csuri got it.

In 1971 he proposed the CGRG at Ohio State, joining faculty and graduate students from art, industrial design, photography and cinema, computer science and mathematics. Starting on an IBM 1130 programmed in FORTRAN, the group worked on hidden-line and shading algorithms and on real-time animation languages. The program seeded two of the prominent real-time computer graphics languages of the next decade, including DeFanti’s GRASS and Manfred Knemeyer’s ANIMA.
An internal NSF report would go on to attribute the greatest impact on computer animation in part to CGRG.

cite.label: Wayne E. Carlson. Computer Graphics and Computer Animation: A Retrospective Overview. p. 103-105. The Ohio State University Press.

img.cap: Charles Csuri working with a light pen at a Vector General display, as reproduced in Carlson's history of computer graphics.
img.credit: Charles Csuri at a Vector General display, from Wayne E. Carlson, Computer Graphics and Computer Animation: A Retrospective Overview (Ohio State University Press). Internet Archive.

body: Following the seminal Pixillation (1970), in 1971 Lillian Schwartz and Ken Knowlton made UFOs at Bell Labs.

It was another film of computer-generated shapes that raced and pulsed across the screen in saturated color, set to a score by Emmanuel Ghent. Like Pixillation, Schwartz again worked the computer output through color filters and an optical printer. The film's rapid alternation of frames was strong enough that viewers reported afterimages of colors that were not on the screen.

With UFOs Schwartz pushed computer film toward perception itself, echoing later work by artists like Kurt Hentschlager. Schwartz went on to make more than thirty films at Bell Labs over the next two productive decades.

img.cap: Ken Knowlton, who programmed UFOs with Lillian Schwartz at Bell Labs, in 2007.
img.credit: Ken Knowlton, Getty Museum, 2007. CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: Neural network research needed a win. It got that and began its long road to recovery after the Perceptrons book setback, especially in the West, with Associative Memory networks.

In 1972 three researchers working separately published network models of associative memory: Teuvo Kohonen in Finland with a “correlation matrix memory,” Kaoru Nakano with the Associatron and James A. Anderson of Rockefeller University in New York with an “interactive memory.” Each stored many patterns across the same set of connections, so that a whole item could be recalled from an associated cue or from a fragment of itself. In other words, computers at the time stored memory like a filing cabinet. These stored memory as distributed, with every memory spread over all the connections.

In the early 1980s Kohonen’s self-organizing map brought Finnish AI research to international attention when Hopfield's 1982 network built directly on this line. Breakthroughs in parallel and distributed computing in earnest would come a decade later but this was a critical step for connectionist, learning AI in an otherwise deep winter.

img.cap: Teuvo Kohonen, one of the three researchers who published associative memory networks in 1972.
img.credit: Teuvo Kohonen, 1980s. Aalto University archives, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: Ah, the era of symbolic AI boom. It continues.

In the fall of 1972, Philippe Roussel implemented the first Prolog in Marseille for Alain Colmerauer’s project to reason with a computer in French. The name, suggested by Roussel’s wife, abbreviates programmation en logique.

A Prolog program was a set of facts and rules in logic. It ran by asking a question it answered by proof, backtracking when a line of reasoning fails. This was not too dissimilar to the English logic program STRIPS, by Richard Fikes and Nils Nilsson at Stanford Research Institute and mentioned previously in this timeline (STRIPS).

The first large Prolog program, 610 clauses by Colmerauer, Robert Pasero and Henry Kanoui, answered questions about short French texts. Prolog was successful enough as Japan’s 1982 Fifth Generation Computer Systems initiative took logic programming, and Prolog in particular, as its basis.

img.cap: Alain Colmerauer, whose Marseille project produced Prolog, in 1988.
img.credit: Alain Colmerauer, July 1988. CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: Is the entire field of AI just fundamentally flawed, asking the wrong questions and making the assumptions from the very beginning?
Today, as the power of these tools has flipped more to, "Uh oh, maybe we should actually be slowing this down," it seems harder to make this point.

But in 1972, it fell on more receptive and convincible ears. Learning and neural nets were "disproven" and expert systems were showing their obvious limitations. The field was vulnerable, even at its very core.
Enter philosopher Hubert L. Dreyfus and his book What Computers Can't Do: A Critique of Artificial Reason.

Dreyfus is like today's Gary Marcus, someone with a long and consistent track record of AI skepticism, regardless of developments. He couldn't be dissuaded because his opposition came from somewhere deep and unmovable.

Marcus (I mean Dreyfus) had begun his attack seven years prior in 1965's “Alchemy and Artificial Intelligence,” a paper for the RAND Corporation. His argument is familiar and persists to this day: That embodiment and experience are fundamental to intelligence.

Drawing on Martin Heidegger and Maurice Merleau-Ponty, he argued that human intelligence depends on bodies, situations and tacit skills that cannot be written down as rules, so the symbolic programs of the day would stall. To be fair, they were correct in predicting the fall of expert systems. But they were less imaginative about the potential of other technologies to be more successful where expert systems failed (hello deep learning and its roots next decade).

So was this the end of AI? As you probably read an AI summary of this text instead of the real thing, obviously not. AI researchers largely dismissed Dreyfus. The guy didn't quit. He doubled down and revised the book as What Computers Still Can't Do in 1992.
My takeaway from these critiques, which have persisted for decades, is to always be wary of saying what computers or machines can never do. Over time, they just might surprise you.

img.cap: The cover of the 1992 revised edition, What Computers Still Can't Do; the 1972 first edition's cover is not openly available.
img.credit: Cover of Hubert L. Dreyfus, What Computers Still Can't Do (MIT Press, 1992), the revised edition of What Computers Can't Do. Open Library.

body: As mentioned, it's the early 1970s and expert systems are all the rage. Learning has fallen out of favor temporarily in the West.
If you wanted AI funding at this time in places like the United States, it had better be symbolic AI.

Work on the symbolic MYCIN began at Stanford in the spring of 1972. It was a collaboration of medical student Edward Shortliffe, computer scientist Bruce Buchanan and clinical pharmacologist Stanley Cohen that became Shortliffe’s 1974 dissertation.

The expert system program advised physicians on antibiotics for bacterial blood infections and, later, meningitis. Its knowledge sat in if-then rules drawn from Cohen and infectious disease physician Stanton Axline, 200 at first and 450 later. MYCIN questioned the physician, reasoned backward from possible conclusions and could show which rule prompted each question. In a blinded 1979 test on ten meningitis cases, eight outside specialists rated it above all nine human prescribers. However, the system was never tested in an actual hospital setting on real people.
Even symbolic AI had limited trust capital, especially when it came to people's health.

img.cap: A portrait of Edward Shortliffe, who built MYCIN as a Stanford medical student.
img.credit: Edward H. Shortliffe. CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: This infamous report is blamed for essentially single-handedly beginning the first AI winter, especially in the UK. It's the best-known example of a direct link to funding drying up (the early robot FREDDY) due to outside skepticism.

By this time in parts of the UK AI funding was growing and fast. But was it really worthwhile? Did any of this computer alchemy even work? There were levels of concern about AI from a very fundamental base at this time.

In early 1973, Britain’s Science Research Council published James Lighthill’s “Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey,” dated July 1972. The council had asked Lighthill, Cambridge’s Lucasian Professor of Applied Mathematics, for a personal review due to his outsider and supposedly unbiased status. He divided the field into advanced automation, computer-based studies of the central nervous system and robot building.

His influential report backed the first two fields, but rejected general robotics. His reasons were issues of scale (sound familiar?) He blamed a failure to recognize the “combinatorial explosion” that swamps search as problems grow. In June 1973 he debated it on BBC television with AI proponents Donald Michie, John McCarthy and Richard Gregory. But the researchers lost the public's and funder's imaginations, as the report spread beyond the UK to places like DARPA, causing a world-wide AI winter (the first AI winter).

img.cap: The cover of the Science Research Council's 1973 paper symposium, which published Lighthill's survey.
img.credit: Cover of Artificial Intelligence: A Paper Symposium (London: Science Research Council, 1973), containing the Lighthill report.

body: While Marvin Minsky's story is so much more complex than the villain of neural networks, in the early 1970s, fresh from his Perceptrons mic drop on the entire field of neural networks, Minsky was still in the villainous symbolic AI phase.

The odd thing about rejecting neural networks is that Minsky was still trying to model what brains did. Rather than modeling based on neuroscience, he made something up called frames. In a June 1974 MIT memo, “A Framework for Representing Knowledge,” Minsky proposed that a mind meeting a new situation, such as a child’s birthday party, selects a remembered structure called a frame and adapts its details to fit.

A frame’s slots come filled with default assumptions that new information can displace. That I guess we can all mostly agree with. But how do they acquire that new information? Can they learn it through training or must it be hard-coded? Minsky went with hard coding.

In 1975 Yale’s Roger Schank and Robert Abelson presented scripts as a specialization of frames: stereotyped action sequences for familiar events. SAM, a program by Chris Riesbeck, Richard Cullingford and Wendy Lehnert, used a restaurant script to fill in a short story’s unstated steps. Their 1977 book Scripts, Plans, Goals and Understanding expanded the theory.
These theories were not entirely without use but they can be considered more cul de sacs than highways.

img.cap: Marvin Minsky in 2006, three decades after his frames memo.
img.credit: Marvin Minsky at the KI 2006 conference. CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: First, with winters, it's important to note that they're more about funding than sentiment per se. Certainly capital and sentiment can go hand in hand. But just because AI capital mostly went away, no doubt damaging spirit, it in no way whatsoever permanently destroyed morale.

Just to recap, from 1969 onwards, AI funding went nearly exclusively to its symbolic, expert system branch. The only issue is that after a few years, that camp's limitations became quite apparent. With apparently nowhere at all for the funds to go as symbolic enthusiasm waned, we enter the first AI winter proper. Now, AI does not completely disappear the rest of the decade as later moments (MYCIN, frames and scripts) will show, but things do get quieter for a bit.

Hard to believe but even the US military with its unlimited budget and keen (KEEN) interest in smarter weapons stopped its funding. The Mansfield Amendment of November 1969 had limited Defense Department support to research of “direct and apparent” military use.

But the real death knell was that pesky Lighthill Report. Its influence extended well beyond the UK as it prompted a Pentagon panel to review DARPA’s own AI program. The result? DARPA moved money out of robotics, hurting Stanford Research Institute. DARPA also ended its five-year Speech Understanding Research program without the planned follow-on.

But it's important to note that AI winters are best thought of as funding dry spells, slower periods, rather than full-fledged cataclysms of nothingness. (again, see the many future moments in this decade about AI). Plenty of evidence suggests that despite wintery conditions, grassroots efforts expanded during this time. The historian Thomas Haigh disputes talk of AI winters and notes that SIGART, the ACM’s AI interest group, grew from 1,241 members in 1973 to 3,500 by mid-1978. People might have cared even if dollars didn't at this time.

img.credit: Senator Mike Mansfield. U.S. Senate, via Wikimedia Commons.
